events.title: Athanasius returns from his first exile
events.summary: Released by Constantine II from exile at Trier after Constantine's death, Athanasius re-entered Alexandria on 23 November 337, but the Eusebian bishops at once accused him of violence and of selling grain meant for widows.

events.title: Second exile of Athanasius; Gregory of Cappadocia installed
events.summary: A synod at Antioch deposed Athanasius again and Constantius had the Cappadocian Gregory installed as bishop by the prefect Philagrius in March 339, amid violence in the churches; Athanasius fled on 16 April to Rome, where he spent seven years under the protection of Pope Julius and Constans.

events.title: Pope Julius' council of Rome acquits Athanasius and Marcellus
events.summary: A synod of some fifty western bishops under Julius I acquitted Athanasius and Marcellus of Ancyra; Julius' letter to the eastern bishops, rebuking them for acting without consulting Rome, is an early statement of Roman appellate authority.

events.title: The Dedication Council of Antioch
events.summary: Some 90-97 eastern bishops gathered with Constantius II to dedicate the Great Church (Golden Octagon) of Antioch, begun by Constantine in 327; they issued four creeds avoiding homoousios, of which the "second creed", said to be Lucian's, became a rallying point, and 25 canons later received into church law.

events.title: Constans' law: "let superstition cease"
events.summary: A law of Constans to the vicar of Italy (CTh 16.10.2) ordered "cesset superstitio, sacrificiorum aboleatur insania", the first imperial prohibition of sacrifice, invoking a (lost) law of Constantine; a law of 342 nevertheless protected temples outside Rome connected with games.
events.debate: Whether Constantine had already issued a general ban on sacrifice is much debated (Barnes vs Bradbury).

events.title: Constans' Frankish war
events.summary: Constans fought the Franks on the lower Rhine in 341-342 and imposed a treaty; Libanius later praised the campaign as having made the Franks quiet.

events.title: Riot at Constantinople; the magister Hermogenes lynched
events.summary: When the magister equitum Hermogenes tried to expel the Nicene bishop Paul in favour of Macedonius, the people burned his house and dragged him through the streets to his death; Constantius rode from Antioch in midwinter, halved the city's free grain allowance and exiled Paul.

events.title: The Macrostich ("long-lined") creed
events.summary: An eastern synod at Antioch sent western bishops in Milan a long, conciliatory creed condemning both Arius' extreme formulas and Marcellus and Photinus, the high-water mark of eastern attempts at compromise before the 350s polarisation.

events.title: Athanasius' triumphal return to Alexandria
events.summary: Pressed by Constans, who threatened war, Constantius allowed Athanasius to return after Gregory's death; he met the emperor at Antioch and entered Alexandria on 21 October 346 to a reception Gregory of Nazianzus compares to an imperial adventus. The following decade was his "golden decade".

events.title: Second Persian siege of Nisibis
events.summary: Shapur II besieged Nisibis again for some 78 days without success; the Chronicle of Edessa and Jerome record the siege, and Ephrem's hymns celebrate the city's survival.

battle.significance: Second failure of Shapur before the fortress.

events.title: The mission of Paul and Macarius and the Bagai massacre
events.summary: Constans sent the commissioners Paul and Macarius to Africa with donations for the poor and pressure for unity; Donatus rejected them ("what has the emperor to do with the church?"), and at Bagai, where Bishop Donatus of Bagai had gathered circumcellions, troops massacred the defenders. Donatist leaders were exiled and the "Macarian times" remembered as persecution.

events.title: FEL TEMP REPARATIO coin reform
events.summary: For Rome's 1100th anniversary in 348 Constans and Constantius issued a new bronze coinage in two or three sizes with a small silver content, carrying the legend FEL(icium) TEMP(orum) REPARATIO ("restoration of happy times") and types such as a soldier spearing a fallen horseman, the phoenix and the emperor on a galley. The large coin was soon reduced and the series debased.

events.title: First Council of Sirmium condemns Photinus
events.summary: Eastern bishops meeting at Sirmium with Constantius deposed the local bishop Photinus, a pupil of Marcellus who taught that Christ was a mere man adopted by God, and issued the First Sirmian Creed with 26 anathemas.

events.title: Gallus made Caesar at Sirmium
events.summary: On 15 March 351 Constantius made his cousin Constantius Gallus, survivor of the 337 massacre, Caesar with residence at Antioch and married him to his sister Constantina, so as to free himself for the war with Magnentius.

events.title: The cross of light over Jerusalem
events.summary: On 7 May 351 a luminous cross was seen over Golgotha stretching to the Mount of Olives; Bishop Cyril reported it to Constantius in a surviving letter as a sign of divine favour in the war against Magnentius. It was probably a solar halo phenomenon.

events.title: Jewish revolt in Galilee
events.summary: Jews of Diocaesarea rose under a certain Patricius (Isaac in some sources), killing soldiers; Gallus' general Ursicinus crushed the revolt, destroying Diocaesarea, Tiberias and Diospolis according to Jerome and Socrates. Archaeology shows destruction at Sepphoris, though much may be due to the earthquake of 363.
events.debate: Scale disputed: rabbinic and archaeological evidence suggests a more limited episode.

events.title: Council of Arles condemns Athanasius
events.summary: Wintering at Arles after his victory, Constantius had Gallic bishops condemn Athanasius; Paulinus of Trier refused and was exiled to Phrygia, and even the papal legate Vincent of Capua signed, to Liberius' dismay.

events.title: Council of Milan; exile of Liberius
events.summary: At Milan in 355 Constantius, reportedly drawing his sword and saying "what I will must be regarded as a canon", forced some 300 bishops to condemn Athanasius; Eusebius of Vercelli, Lucifer of Cagliari and Dionysius of Milan refused and were exiled, and Pope Liberius, who also refused, was taken from Rome to Beroea in Thrace.

events.title: Constantius against Gundomad and Vadomar
events.summary: Constantius marched to the Rhine near Augst against the Alamannic brother-kings Gundomad and Vadomar, but finding the crossing blocked made peace; in 355 his magister Arbitio was ambushed by the Lentienses near Lake Constance before winning a victory.

events.title: Franks capture Cologne
events.summary: In late 355, after a long siege, a large Frankish force took and sacked Cologne; with the murder of Silvanus the Rhine defences collapsed, and some 40-45 towns were reported in barbarian hands when Julian arrived in Gaul. Julian retook the city in 356.

battle.significance: Symbol of the collapse of Rhine defences that made Julian's Caesarship necessary.

events.title: Julian's victory at Brocomagus
events.summary: Julian's first battle: marching from Autun via Auxerre and Troyes to Reims and then into Alsace, he repelled an Alamannic attack at Brocomagus by enveloping them with his two wings, after an earlier ambush of his rearguard near Decem Pagi. He then recovered Cologne and made peace with the Frankish kings.

battle.significance: Julian's first field success, restoring confidence in the Gallic army.

events.title: Julian besieged at Senones
events.summary: Wintering at Sens with few troops, Julian was besieged for thirty days by Alamanni while the magister equitum Marcellus, nearby, failed to help; Julian had Marcellus dismissed, beginning his fight for control of the Gallic command.

events.title: Third exile of Athanasius: the night attack on the church of Theonas
events.summary: On the night of 8-9 February 356 the dux Syrianus with 5,000 soldiers surrounded the church of Theonas during a vigil; Athanasius escaped in the crowd and spent six years hidden among the monks of Egypt, writing his Apologies and the History of the Arians, while George of Cappadocia was installed as bishop (February 357).

events.title: Constantius orders temples closed and sacrifice punished with death
events.summary: Laws of 356 (CTh 16.10.4 and 16.10.6) ordered temples closed in all places and cities and threatened capital punishment and confiscation for sacrifice or the worship of images. Enforcement was sporadic: Constantius himself admired the temples of Rome in 357.
events.debate: The date of 16.10.4 (346, 354 or 356) is uncertain.

events.title: Constantius removes the Altar of Victory from the Curia
events.summary: During his visit to Rome in 357 Constantius had the statue and altar of Victory, set up by Augustus after Actium, removed from the Senate house, because senators burned incense on it at meetings; it was restored, probably under Julian, and became the symbol of the pagan senators' resistance in 382-394.

events.title: Constantius raises an obelisk in the Circus Maximus
events.summary: The obelisk of Thutmose III and IV from Karnak, which Constantine had planned to bring to Constantinople, was shipped to Rome on a specially built vessel and erected on the spina of the Circus Maximus in 357; at 32 m (without base) it is the tallest standing ancient obelisk, re-erected at the Lateran in 1588.

events.title: Defeat of Barbatio near Augst
events.summary: In the pincer plan of 357 the magister peditum Barbatio advanced with 25,000 men from Italy to Rauracum, but refused to cooperate with Julian, was surprised by the Alamanni and driven back with the loss of his baggage, leaving Julian to face Chnodomar alone at Strasbourg.

sides.losses: baggage, pack animals and camp followers

events.title: Julian besieges Franks in the Meuse forts
events.summary: After Strasbourg, 600 Frankish raiders shut themselves in two abandoned forts on the Meuse; Julian besieged them for 54 days in midwinter, breaking the river ice each night, until they surrendered and were sent to Constantius as recruits.

events.title: The Second Creed of Sirmium (the "Blasphemy")
events.summary: A small group of western bishops (Ursacius, Valens, Germinius, Potamius) at Sirmium forbade the use of ousia, homoousios and homoiousios and declared the Father greater than the Son; the aged Ossius of Cordoba signed under pressure. Hilary called it the "Blasphemy", and it drove moderate easterners into the homoiousian camp under Basil of Ancyra.

events.title: Earthquake destroys Nicomedia
events.summary: At dawn on 24 August 358 an earthquake followed by fire destroyed Nicomedia, Diocletian's capital; Ammianus describes the catastrophe and Libanius wrote a monody for the city, where the vicar Aristaenetus died in the ruins. A synod planned there was moved, eventually becoming the twin councils of 359.

events.title: Julian subdues the Salian Franks and Chamavi
events.summary: Julian accepted the surrender of the Salian Franks settled in Toxandria, allowing them to stay as subjects, and drove back the Chamavi, opening the Rhine to grain ships from Britain (600 ships, says Julian) and rebuilding forts at Castra Herculis, Quadriburgium and Novaesium.

events.title: Constantius against the Limigantes
events.summary: Constantius campaigned from Sirmium against the Sarmatians and Quadi in 358, restored the "free" Sarmatians under a client king Zizais, and attacked the Limigantes, their former serfs; in 359 a parley with the Limigantes near Acimincum turned into a massacre when they attacked the emperor's tribunal.

events.title: Basil of Ancyra's homoiousian synod
events.summary: Alarmed by the Anomoean teaching of Aetius and Eunomius, Basil of Ancyra assembled bishops before Easter 358 who declared the Son "like in essence" (homoiousios) to the Father; Constantius briefly backed them and exiled Aetius.

events.title: The sarcophagus of Junius Bassus
events.summary: Junius Bassus, prefect of Rome, died in office on 25 August 359 aged 42, "newly baptised", and was buried near St Peter's in a marble sarcophagus whose two registers of biblical scenes, with Christ enthroned above Caelus, are a masterpiece of early Christian sculpture.

events.title: Homoian council of Constantinople
events.summary: In January 360 a council at Constantinople ratified the Homoian creed of Rimini and Seleucia ("the Son is like the Father according to the Scriptures"), deposed Basil of Ancyra and other homoiousians, and made Eudoxius bishop of the capital; Ulfilas attended. This creed was the faith the Goths received.

events.title: Dedication of the first Hagia Sophia
events.summary: The Great Church (Megale Ekklesia) of Constantinople, begun under Constantine, was dedicated on 15 February 360 by the newly installed Homoian bishop Eudoxius; a timber-roofed basilica, it burned in the riots over John Chrysostom's exile in 404.

events.title: Julian's march down the Danube
events.summary: Breaking with Constantius, Julian sent columns through Italy and Raetia while he himself boarded river boats with 3,000 men and sailed down the Danube, reaching Sirmium in October 361 to a surprised welcome, then held the Succi pass and waited at Naissus, where news of Constantius' death arrived.

events.title: The tribunal of Chalcedon
events.summary: In December 361 Julian set up a commission at Chalcedon under Salutius Secundus, with army officers including Arbitio, Nevitta and Jovinus, to try Constantius' ministers; the grand chamberlain Eusebius and the notary Paul "the Chain" were burned alive, but the execution of the finance minister Ursulus shocked even Ammianus.

events.title: Lynching of George of Cappadocia
events.summary: When news of Constantius' death arrived, the Alexandrian mob dragged the hated Arian bishop George, who had sneered at the temple of the Genius of the city, from prison, killed him with two officials on 24 December 361, paraded his body on a camel and burned it. Julian rebuked the city but claimed George's library.

events.title: Julian's edict on teachers
events.summary: A law of 17 June 362 (CTh 13.3.5) required civic approval for teachers, and an accompanying letter argued that Christians who did not believe in the gods could not honestly teach Homer and Hesiod and should "go to the churches of the Galilaeans and expound Matthew and Luke". Marius Victorinus and Prohaeresius resigned; Ammianus called it harsh and best buried in silence.

events.title: Athanasius' "Council of the Confessors" at Alexandria
events.summary: Returned under Julian's amnesty, Athanasius held a small synod which accepted repentant Arians, affirmed the divinity of the Holy Spirit and recognised that "one hypostasis" and "three hypostases" could be orthodox if properly understood, laying the groundwork for the Cappadocian settlement; Lucifer of Cagliari rejected it.

events.title: Fourth exile of Athanasius under Julian
events.summary: Angered that Athanasius was baptising pagan women of rank, Julian ordered him expelled on 23 October 362 as a "disturber of the peace"; Athanasius told his followers it was "a little cloud that will pass" and hid on the Nile until Julian's death.

events.title: Julian storms Pirisabora
events.summary: Marching down the Euphrates with 65,000 men and a fleet of 1,100 ships, Julian took the strong city of Pirisabora after two days of assault, Julian himself trying to batter a gate under a hail of missiles; the garrison of 2,500 surrendered and the city was burned.

battle.significance: Opened the road down the Euphrates towards Ctesiphon.

events.title: Julian burns his fleet
events.summary: Unable to take Ctesiphon and misled, Ammianus hints, by Persian deserters, Julian ordered his river fleet burned except for a few boats so that 20,000 men would not be needed to tow it upstream, and turned inland; the decision is judged among his worst.

events.title: Battle of Maranga
events.summary: On 22 June 363 the retreating Roman army fought a pitched battle at Maranga with a Persian army under Merena with cataphracts and elephants; Julian closed quickly to avoid the archers and won, but could not stop the harassment that killed him four days later.

sides.strength: army under Merena with cataphracts and elephants

battle.significance: Tactical success that did not change the strategic trap.

events.title: Julian writes Against the Galilaeans
events.summary: In the winter of 362-363 at Antioch Julian composed three books attacking Christianity as an apostasy from both Hellenism and Judaism; the work survives only in fragments quoted in Cyril of Alexandria's refutation of the 430s. The same winter he wrote the Misopogon against the Antiochenes.
